rows.label: Concept
rows.text: A **potential divider** — two series resistors across a source — delivers an output fraction of the input: $V_{out} = V\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}$; a potentiometer makes the fraction continuously adjustable (volume controls, dimmers). rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - V_out = V R₂/(R₁+R₂) - Potentiometer: E₁/E₂ = l₁/l₂ - Drop per length k = IR_uniform

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **No-Load Assumption:** The simple voltage divider formula $V_{out} = V_{in} \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$ assumes the output current is zero (infinite load resistance). Any load drawing current changes the effective resistance of the lower branch.  ·  **Loading Effect Formalism:** When a load $R_L$ is connected across $R_2$, the effective resistance becomes $R_2' = R_2 \parallel R_L = \frac{R_2 R_L}{R_2 + R_L}$. The new output voltage is $V_{out} = V_{in} \frac{R_2'}{R_1 + R_2'}$.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Tapping a Fraction of a Voltage Two resistors in series across a battery form a voltage tap: the junction sits at a fixed fraction of the supply. Slide the tap (a rheostat) and you have a volume control, a dimmer, a sensor readout — the potential divider is electronics' most humble workhorse.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 The divider formula Two resistors R₁ and R₂ in series across a source V. The same current I = V/(R₁+R₂) flows through both; the voltage across R₂ is: $$V_{out} = V \times \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$$ — the output is a fixed *fraction* of the input, set purely by the resistance ratio.…  ·  ## 3. Conceptual Relationships - **To Topic 101:** the divider is a series pair; the current is common. - **To Topic 103:** the potentiometer beats a voltmeter because it draws no current — no internal-resistance error. - **To sensors:** LDRs and thermistors in a divider convert light and heat into voltage.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Design Trade-off:** To minimize loading effects, the divider resistance ($R_1 + R_2$) should be much smaller than $R_L$. However, this increases power dissipation ($P = V_{in}^2/(R_1 + R_2)$). The designer must balance voltage stability against power efficiency.  ·  Note 3: Practice numerical problems regularly for mastery of Potential Divider  ·  Note 4: Remember the units and dimensions involved in Potential Divider
